subject: DI02000121

intro_text.en: Unit 6 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) introduces Computer-Aided Drafting: the CAD software available and what it can do, the AutoCAD window part by part, file operations, setting up a drawing (units, limits, grid, snap and the status-bar aids), the coordinate systems used to enter points exactly, and the organising concepts of layers, blocks and hatch. Unit 7 then dimensions the CAD drawing; Practical 7 produces a plotted 2D drawing in AutoCAD.

title.en: 6.1-6.3 CAD software, the AutoCAD window and file features
title.gu: 6.1-6.3 CAD software, the AutoCAD window and file features

h.en: 6.1 CAD software in the field and their capabilities
h.gu: 6.1 CAD software in the field and their capabilities

body.en:
What CAD replaced - and what it did not

CAD (Computer-Aided Design/Drafting) software produces the same standardised drawings of Units 1-5 on a computer: exact geometry (no scale-rule error), instant editing (move/copy/mirror instead of erasing), reuse (blocks, templates, copied details), automatic hatching/dimensioning assistance, layer-based organisation, and clean plotted output at any scale. The conventions do not change - line types, sections, symbols and GD&T of the earlier units are exactly what the software must produce; CAD replaces the pencil, never the drafting knowledge.

The software landscape

  • AutoCAD (Autodesk): the general-purpose 2D drafting standard taught in this course; also 3D modelling; DWG file format is the industry exchange format.
  • Parametric 3D modellers: SolidWorks, Autodesk Inventor, Creo, CATIA, NX - parts are modelled as solids with parameters and drawings are generated/updated from the model; used for product design.
  • Free/open and light tools: LibreCAD, DraftSight/FreeCAD, nanoCAD - 2D capability for viewing, teaching and small work.
  • Capability ladder: 2D drafting (this course) -> 3D solid/surface modelling -> assembly modelling with interference checks -> CAM/CAE links (machining toolpaths, stress analysis) -> PLM data management in large companies.

body.en:
Tour of the window (diagram md6_window)

  • Title bar: application and drawing names (Drawing1.dwg until saved), with the application menu button 'A'.
  • Quick Access Toolbar: New, Open, Save, Save As, Undo, Redo - one click, customisable.
  • Ribbon: tabs (Home, Insert, Annotate, Parametric, View, Manage...) each holding panels of tools - Draw panel (Line, Circle, Arc, Polyline...), Modify panel (Move, Copy, Rotate, Mirror, Trim, Fillet...), Layers, Annotation. The ribbon is the modern replacement of the classical Draw and Modify toolbars (floating/docked toolbars of the older interface - same commands).
  • Drawing area (viewport): the sheet of infinite size where geometry is drawn at true size (1 unit = 1 mm by setup); crosshair cursor; UCS icon at the origin shows the X-Y axes directions; ViewCube/NavBar navigate views (zoom/pan).
  • Command prompt/window: the conversation line - commands are typed here (or picked from ribbon) and AutoCAD prompts for points/options step by step. Reading the command line is the core operating skill: every tool explains itself there.
  • Status bar: Model/Layout tabs and the drafting-aid toggles - GRID, SNAP, ORTHO, POLAR, OSNAP, DYN (dynamic input), LWT (lineweight), ISODRAFT (Card 6.4) - plus coordinate readout.

Command entry - three equivalent ways

Ribbon icon, typed command name or its alias (L for LINE, C for CIRCLE, M for MOVE), or right-click menus; Enter repeats the last command; Esc cancels. The drawing aids can be toggled by status-bar buttons or function keys (F7 grid, F9 snap, F8 ortho, F3 osnap, F12 dynamic input).

body.en:
The file operations

  • New (NEW/QNEW): starts a drawing, normally from a template (.dwt) carrying preset units, limits, layers, text/dimension styles and a title block - the CAD equivalent of opening a fresh standard sheet.
  • Save (SAVE/QSAVE): writes the .dwg file; first save asks name and location. Save early and often - CAD files are the master record. Save As creates copies/versions or other formats (older DWG versions, DXF for exchange with other software).
  • Open (OPEN): loads an existing .dwg; recent-file list and previews aid finding. Backup (.bak) and auto-save (.sv$) files protect work against crashes.

Good file habits (examined as practice)

Meaningful file names with revision (Flange_Drilling_R2.dwg), one project folder per job, templates for every new sheet, and plots (PDF/DWF) for issue - the recipient of a plotted PDF can read/print without AutoCAD, exactly like a printed A2 sheet.

h.en: 6.4 Setting up a new drawing: units, limits and the drawing aids
h.gu: 6.4 Setting up a new drawing: units, limits and the drawing aids

body.en:
Setup sequence for every new drawing

  • UNITS: set the drawing unit and precision - for mechanical work: decimal millimetres, precision 0.0 or 0.00; angle in decimal degrees. One drawing unit = 1 mm thereafter.
  • LIMITS: the intended drawing extent (e.g. 0,0 to 420,297 for an A3 field, or comfortably around the part) - grid displays inside limits, and ZOOM All frames them.
  • GRID (F7): visible dot pattern at set spacing - a visual ruler, never printed. SNAP (F9): forces the cursor to jump in set steps for quick regular layouts; grid and snap spacing are set independently.

The accuracy aids (this is where CAD beats the pencil)

  • ORTHO (F8): constrains lines horizontal/vertical. POLAR tracking: snaps to set angles (30/45/90 deg...) with alignment paths - ORTHO's angular generalisation.
  • OSNAP (F3) - object snap: grabs exact geometric points of existing objects: ENDpoint, MIDpoint, CENtre, INTersection, PERpendicular, TANgent, NEArest... - the difference between a drawing that merely looks right and one that is right. Running osnaps are set with the OSNAP dialog; markers (square=endpoint, triangle=midpoint, circle=centre) confirm the grab.
  • DYNMODE (F12, dynamic input): dimension/angle boxes at the cursor while drawing - values are typed where the eyes are.
  • ISODRAFT: switches the crosshair/grid to isometric planes (left/right/top) for isometric pictorial drawing; Dynamic UCS: automatically aligns the XY plane to a face of a 3D solid while modelling.

h.en: 6.5 Coordinate systems in AutoCAD: absolute, relative, Cartesian and polar
h.gu: 6.5 Coordinate systems in AutoCAD: absolute, relative, Cartesian and polar

body.en:
Points are entered as coordinates - four ways

The drawing plane is the XY plane of the World Coordinate System (WCS), origin (0,0) at the UCS icon (a User Coordinate System can relocate it). Every point AutoCAD asks for can be typed as:

  • Absolute Cartesian: X,Y measured from the origin - '30,15' is the point 30 right, 15 up, always.
  • Relative Cartesian: @dx,dy measured from the last point entered - '@30,15' means 30 right and 15 up from where you are; the @ is the whole meaning. Most real drawing is relative.
  • Absolute polar: distance<angle from the origin - '50<30'.
  • Relative polar: @distance<angle from the last point - '@40<30' draws a 40-long line at 30 deg. Polar is the natural input for inclined lines, chamfers and bolt circles.

Worked trace (diagram)

LINE from P1 (0,0): enter 30,15 (absolute) for P2 - or @30,15 - then @40<30 reaches P3 = (30 + 40 cos 30, 15 + 40 sin 30) = (64.6, 35). Two habits make coordinate entry reliable: watch the command-line prompt (it tells which point is wanted), and verify with the coordinate readout/DIST command instead of trusting the screen scale.

h.en: 6.6 Layers, blocks and hatch - organising the drawing
h.gu: 6.6 Layers, blocks and hatch - organising the drawing

body.en:
Layers: transparent sheets, one per kind of information

A layer is a named drawing level carrying its own colour, linetype and lineweight; every object is drawn on a layer. A disciplined mechanical drawing uses layers such as OBJECT (visible outlines), CENTRE, HIDDEN, DIM (dimensions), HATCH, TITLE - echoing the line language of Unit 1. Layer controls per layer: On/Off (invisible, still processed), Freeze (invisible and skipped - faster), Lock (visible, uneditable), colour/linetype/lineweight assignment, and Plot/No-plot. Benefits: switch off dimensions to read geometry, plot construction lines away, change a whole class (all centre lines green) in one edit, and keep a large drawing navigable.

Blocks: draw once, insert many times

A block is a named group of objects defined once (BLOCK command: base point + objects) and inserted (INSERT) any number of times at any scale/rotation: bolts, nuts, weld and roughness symbols, the title block itself. Editing the definition updates every insert; blocks keep file size small and symbols standard. (Dynamic blocks add stretch/flip parameters; block attributes carry text data such as part numbers.)

Hatch: filling closed areas

HATCH fills a closed boundary with a pattern (ANSI31 = the 45 deg section lining of Unit 2, plus steel/concrete/earth material patterns), with angle and scale controls; associative hatch updates when the boundary is edited. On mechanical drawings hatch is used almost entirely for sectional views - placed on its own HATCH layer.

h.en: Q1. What is CAD? State four advantages of CAD over manual drafting.
h.gu: Q1. What is CAD? State four advantages of CAD over manual drafting.

body.en:
Model answer

CAD (Computer-Aided Design/Drafting) is the preparation of engineering drawings with computer software (AutoCAD for 2D drafting in this course). Advantages: (1) accuracy - geometry is created from exact coordinates and object snaps, free of scale-rule and pencil error; (2) speed of editing - move/copy/mirror/trim replace erasing and redrawing, so revisions take minutes; (3) reuse and standardisation - blocks, templates and layers keep symbols and sheets uniform and reusable across projects; (4) output quality and sharing - clean plots at any scale, PDF issue, and DWG/DXF exchange between companies. The drafting conventions (lines, sections, symbols, GD&T) remain the same as manual work; CAD strengthens their execution.

h.en: Q3. Explain: GRID, SNAP, ORTHO and OSNAP modes.
h.gu: Q3. Explain: GRID, SNAP, ORTHO and OSNAP modes.

body.en:
Model answer

GRID (F7) displays a pattern of dots at a set spacing inside the drawing limits as a visual reference; it does not print. SNAP (F9) restricts cursor movement to a set step so points land on a regular lattice. ORTHO (F8) constrains lines and moves to horizontal/vertical directions only. OSNAP (F3), object snap, picks exact geometric points on existing objects - endpoint (square marker), midpoint (triangle), centre (circle), intersection, perpendicular, tangent - which is what makes CAD geometry exact rather than approximate. GRID/SNAP help layout by eye; OSNAP guarantees connection accuracy.

h.en: Q4. Differentiate between absolute, relative Cartesian and relative polar coordinates, with examples.
h.gu: Q4. Differentiate between absolute, relative Cartesian and relative polar coordinates, with examples.

body.en:
Model answer

Absolute Cartesian (30,15): the point is always 30 units in X and 15 in Y from the WCS origin (0,0), regardless of history. Relative Cartesian (@30,15): 30 in X and 15 in Y measured from the last point entered - the @ changes the reference from the origin to the current point. Relative polar (@40<30): a point 40 units away from the last point at 30 degrees to the X axis - the natural form for drawing an inclined line of known length. Example trace: from (0,0), @30,15 then @40<30 ends at (64.6, 35). Relative entry dominates practical drawing because parts are dimensioned from feature to feature, not from a distant origin.

Model answer

Example trace: from (0,0), @30,15 then @40<30 ends at (64.6, 35). Relative entry dominates practical drawing because parts are dimensioned from feature to feature, not from a distant origin.

h.en: Q5. What are layers? State four layer properties/controls.
h.gu: Q5. What are layers? State four layer properties/controls.

body.en:
Model answer

A layer is a named, transparent level of the drawing with its own colour, linetype and lineweight, on which related objects are drawn (OBJECT, CENTRE, HIDDEN, DIM, HATCH, TITLE...). Controls: On/Off - hide or show the layer's objects (still processed when off); Freeze/Thaw - hide and exclude from processing for speed in big drawings; Lock/Unlock - visible but protected from editing; Plot/No-plot - exclude construction layers from the printed sheet. Colour/linetype/lineweight can also be set per layer so classes of lines change together (ByLayer discipline).

h.en: Q6. What is a block in AutoCAD? Give two applications.
h.gu: Q6. What is a block in AutoCAD? Give two applications.

body.en:
Model answer

A block is a named group of objects defined once with a base (insertion) point and then inserted repeatedly at any position, scale or rotation with the INSERT command; editing the block definition updates all its inserts. Applications: (1) standard symbols and fasteners - bolts, nuts, weld/roughness symbols inserted identically everywhere; (2) the title block with border, inserted on every sheet of a project so all sheets match. Blocks standardise content, reduce file size and make global changes in one edit.

h.en: Q7. Write the setup sequence for starting a new mechanical drawing in AutoCAD.
h.gu: Q7. Write the setup sequence for starting a new mechanical drawing in AutoCAD.

body.en:

(1) NEW from the metric template; (2) UNITS - decimal millimetres, required precision, degree angles; (3) LIMITS to suit the part/sheet and ZOOM All; (4) GRID and SNAP spacings as convenient multiples; (5) OSNAP running modes (endpoint, midpoint, centre, intersection) and DYN on; (6) create the LAYERS (object, centre, hidden, dimension, hatch) with colours/linetypes; (7) set text and dimension styles (Unit 7); then draw at full true size (1 unit = 1 mm) and SAVE with a proper name in the project folder.

h.en: Q8. What is the UCS icon? What is Dynamic UCS?
h.gu: Q8. What is the UCS icon? What is Dynamic UCS?

body.en:
Model answer

The UCS icon is the small X-Y axes marker displayed at the origin of the current User Coordinate System in the drawing area; it shows where (0,0) is and which way X and Y point, so coordinate entry is never disoriented. Dynamic UCS is a 3D-modelling aid that temporarily aligns the UCS XY-plane automatically onto a face of a solid as the cursor moves over it, letting the user draw directly on that face without manually redefining the UCS.

name.en: Modify commands (command - alias - what it does)
name.gu: Modify commands (command - alias - what it does)

body.en:
MOVE (M) - shift objects ; COPY (CO) - duplicate ; ROTATE (RO) - turn about a base point ; MIRROR (MI) - reflect about a line ; OFFSET (O) - parallel copy at distance ; TRIM (TR) / EXTEND (EX) - cut/lengthen to boundaries ; FILLET (F) / CHAMFER (CHA) - round/corner edges ; SCALE (SC) - resize by factor ; STRETCH (S) - pull a windowed part ; ARRAY (AR) - rectangular/polar patterns ; ERASE (E) - delete

Modify commands first ask 'Select objects' - window left-to-right selects only fully-enclosed objects; right-to-left (crossing) selects everything touched.

MOVE (M) - shift objects ; COPY (CO) - duplicate ; ROTATE (RO) - turn about a base point ; MIRROR (MI) - reflect about a line ; OFFSET (O) - parallel copy at distance ; TRIM (TR) / EXTEND (EX) - cut/lengthen to boundaries ; FILLET (F) / CHAMFER (CHA) - round/corner edges ; SCALE (SC) - resize by factor ; STRETCH (S) - pull a windowed part ; ARRAY (AR) - rectangular/polar patterns ; ERASE (E) - delete

Modify commands first ask 'Select objects' - window left-to-right selects only fully-enclosed objects; right-to-left (crossing) selects everything touched.

h.gu: Modify commands (command - alias - what it does)

body.en:
F3 OSNAP - F7 GRID - F8 ORTHO - F9 SNAP - F10 POLAR - F12 DYNAMIC INPUT ; Enter = repeat last command ; Esc = cancel

Aliases save the most time: L, C, A, M, CO, RO, MI, O, TR, F, E, Z (ZOOM), P (PAN).

q.en: Full form of CAD and UCS?
q.gu: Full form of CAD and UCS?

a.en: CAD: Computer-Aided Design/Drafting. UCS: User Coordinate System - the relocatable XY working plane whose origin the UCS icon marks.
a.gu: CAD: Computer-Aided Design/Drafting. UCS: User Coordinate System - the relocatable XY working plane whose origin the UCS icon marks.

q.en: Which file formats does AutoCAD save?
q.gu: Which file formats does AutoCAD save?

a.en: Native .dwg; templates .dwt; exchange format .dxf; plus .bak backups, .sv$ autosaves, and PDF/DWF plots for issue.
a.gu: Native .dwg; templates .dwt; exchange format .dxf; plus .bak backups, .sv$ autosaves, and PDF/DWF plots for issue.

q.en: GRID vs SNAP?
q.gu: GRID vs SNAP?

a.en: GRID only displays reference dots (not printed, no control of the cursor); SNAP actually forces the cursor to step in set increments.
a.gu: GRID only displays reference dots (not printed, no control of the cursor); SNAP actually forces the cursor to step in set increments.

q.en: Why is OSNAP more important than SNAP for accuracy?
q.gu: Why is OSNAP more important than SNAP for accuracy?

a.en: OSNAP picks mathematically exact points of existing geometry (endpoint, centre...). A drawing connected by OSNAP is exact; SNAP alone only lands on a regular lattice and can miss the intended feature.
a.gu: OSNAP picks mathematically exact points of existing geometry (endpoint, centre...). A drawing connected by OSNAP is exact; SNAP alone only lands on a regular lattice and can miss the intended feature.

q.en: ORTHO vs POLAR tracking?
q.gu: ORTHO vs POLAR tracking?

a.en: ORTHO restricts to horizontal/vertical only. POLAR generalises it: alignment paths at chosen angle increments (e.g. every 30 deg), so inclined lines snap too.
a.gu: ORTHO restricts to horizontal/vertical only. POLAR generalises it: alignment paths at chosen angle increments (e.g. every 30 deg), so inclined lines snap too.

q.en: What does the @ symbol do in coordinate entry?
q.gu: What does the @ symbol do in coordinate entry?

a.en: It makes the entry relative to the last point instead of the origin: @30,15 or @40<30.
a.gu: It makes the entry relative to the last point instead of the origin: @30,15 or @40<30.

q.en: Layer Freeze vs Off?
q.gu: Layer Freeze vs Off?

a.en: Off hides objects but AutoCAD still processes them (regenerates, zooms to them). Freeze also excludes them from processing - faster in large drawings.
a.gu: Off hides objects but AutoCAD still processes them (regenerates, zooms to them). Freeze also excludes them from processing - faster in large drawings.

q.en: Block vs group of copied objects?
q.gu: Block vs group of copied objects?

a.en: A block is one definition inserted many times: edit the definition and every insert updates; inserts keep the file small and standard. Copies are independent objects.
a.gu: A block is one definition inserted many times: edit the definition and every insert updates; inserts keep the file small and standard. Copies are independent objects.

q.en: What is a template (.dwt) file?
q.gu: What is a template (.dwt) file?

a.en: A pre-set starting drawing - units, limits, layers, styles, border/title block - so every new drawing of a company starts identically.
a.gu: A pre-set starting drawing - units, limits, layers, styles, border/title block - so every new drawing of a company starts identically.

q.en: ISODRAFT is used for what?
q.gu: ISODRAFT is used for what?

a.en: Isometric pictorial drawing: it tilts the grid/crosshair to the isometric planes (left/right/top) with isoplane switching.
a.gu: Isometric pictorial drawing: it tilts the grid/crosshair to the isometric planes (left/right/top) with isoplane switching.

q.en: Name the Draw and Modify commands for: parallel copy, reflection, pattern.
q.gu: Name the Draw and Modify commands for: parallel copy, reflection, pattern.

a.en: OFFSET (parallel copy at a distance), MIRROR (reflection about a mirror line), ARRAY (rectangular/polar repeated pattern).
a.gu: OFFSET (parallel copy at a distance), MIRROR (reflection about a mirror line), ARRAY (rectangular/polar repeated pattern).

q.en: Command line - why watch it?
q.gu: Command line - why watch it?

a.en: It is AutoCAD's conversation: after every pick it states the next input wanted and the options in [brackets]. Most beginner errors are simply not reading it.
a.gu: It is AutoCAD's conversation: after every pick it states the next input wanted and the options in [brackets]. Most beginner errors are simply not reading it.
